## {.center}

::: {style="font-size: 1.3em; line-height: 1.3;"}
Most data pipelines are an ordered
list of function calls.

{workr} takes that literally.
:::

::: {.notes}
30-min talk + 10-min Q&A. The framing, stated plainly: a workflow is a list of
function calls written as config. The next 20 minutes show that this small idea
holds up at three scales — a toy calc, a regulated production system, and the
whole pharmaverse stack. Timing: intro ~3, scale ~5, pharmaverse ~8,
AI + what's new ~3, close ~1.
:::

## A complete pipeline

```{.yaml code-line-numbers="|2-4|5-14|"}
# hello_cars.yaml
meta:
  ID: hello_cars
  col: speed
steps:
  - name: dplyr::pull
    output: speed
    params:
      df: df
      col: col
  - name: mean
    output: result
    params:
      lData: speed
```

::: {.notes}
Reveal 1: the whole file. Reveal 2: `meta` is metadata. Reveal 3: `steps` is an
ordered list of function calls, each with an `output` and `params`. There isn't
much more framework than what's on the slide.
:::

## The model

::: {.tocbox}
- A **workflow** is a YAML list of function calls
- **`lData`** flows through every step and is updated as it goes
- **`workr::RunWorkflow()`** runs the list and returns the last result
:::

::: {.notes}
`RunWorkflows()` (plural) chains workflows; each output feeds the next `lData`.
Keep this slide brief — it's the contract.
:::

## Configuration, not code

![](images/example1.png)

::: {.notes}
`workr::demoApp()`. If live: change `col` from `speed` to `dist` — the result
updates and the steps stay put. The logic is data you can edit, diff, and
review rather than a script you rewrite. Point: declarative definitions are
easier for others to trust and audit.
:::

# Does this scale? {.center}

## The starting point: a script per study {.full-image-slide}

![](images/safetyGraphics_config.png){fig-alt="A large, gnarly study configuration"}

<p class="img-caption">One study. Now imagine thirty, changing every month.</p>

::: {.notes}
~5:00. The motivation. Clinical trials are complex: study designs vary and
metrics need study- and sometimes metric-level tweaks. Hand-written per-study
scripts became hard to maintain, and existing tools (`targets`, `glue`) felt
heavier than we wanted.
:::

## Why per-study scripts didn't hold up

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em; line-height: 1.4;"}
30 studies × monthly snapshots
× 15 metrics × 5 steps
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.5em; margin-top: 0.4em;"}
≈ 27,000 metrics / year
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.72em; opacity:0.8; margin-top:0.5em;"}
…and each one is regulated, GxP output.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the practical reason workr exists. Hand-auditing tens of thousands of
bespoke scripts a year isn't feasible; auditing one framework plus many small
configs is.
:::

## One framework instead of many scripts

- Every metric became the same workflow shape — only `params` differ
- Built `gsm::RunWorkflow()` in **April 2022**, later extracted **`{workr}`**
- Qualified once, via [{qcthat}](https://github.com/Gilead-BioStats/qcthat) —
  now running **20+ studies** in production

![](images/data_analysis.png){width=62%}

::: {.notes}
Same five steps for every KRI; the metric is expressed through its params.
Qualify the framework once rather than validating thousands of scripts — that
is the payoff for describing pipelines as configuration.
:::

# The same approach across {pharmaverse} {.center}

::: {style="opacity:0.8; font-size:0.85em;"}
not only clinical operations
:::

::: {.notes}
~10:00. Second point: breadth. The same workflow shape maps onto the standard
clinical data flow, and none of it is workr-specific.
:::

## One pattern, the whole clinical stack {.center}

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; line-height: 1.5;"}
**RAW** → **SDTM** → **ADaM** → **TFL / ARD**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.78em; opacity: 0.85; margin-top: 0.6em;"}
`{sdtm.oak}` · `{admiral}` · `{rmarkdown}` · `{cards}`
:::

::: {.notes}
Each arrow is more steps. Each package is a set of functions, and a function
call is a step — so the packages you already know are the pipeline.
:::

## A step is a function call {.step1-compare}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Workflow step
```yaml
steps:
  - output: vs_raw2
    name: sdtm.oak::generate_oak_id_vars
    params:
      raw_dat: vs_raw
      pat_var: "PATNUM"
      raw_src: "vitals"
```
:::
::: {.column width="4%"}
=
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
Plain R
```R
vs_raw2 <-
  generate_oak_id_vars(
    raw_dat = vs_raw,
    pat_var = "PATNUM",
    raw_src = "vitals"
  )
```
:::
:::

Adopting a package is mostly about knowing that package, not learning {workr}.

::: {.notes}
The anchor slide for this section: show one mapping in full so the equivalence
is clear, then let the audience extrapolate the rest rather than repeating it.
:::

## The rest of the stack follows the same form {.smaller}

| Stage | Package | A representative step |
|---|---|---|
| SDTM → ADaM | `{admiral}` | `admiral::derive_param_map()` → MAP from SYSBP/DIABP |
| ADaM → TFL | `{rmarkdown}` | `rmarkdown::render()` a parameterized template |
| ADaM → ARD | `{cards}` | `cards::ard_summary()` for CDISC Analysis Results Data |

::: {style="font-size:0.72em; opacity:0.85; margin-top:0.4em;"}
`!expr` carries quasiquotation (`exprs()`, `!!`) directly into a step's params.
:::

::: {.notes}
This condenses what used to be three near-identical YAML-vs-R slides. If the
room wants depth on any row, that's what Q&A and the long-form Phuse Connect
deck are for.
:::

## Example: a summary in two steps {.center}

```yaml
steps:
  - output: predose_map
    name: workr::RunQuery      # SQL over a data.frame
    params:
      df: ADVS
      strQuery: "SELECT * FROM df WHERE PARAMCD='MAP' AND VISIT='VISIT1'"
  - output: table_map
    name: cards::ard_summary   # CDISC ARD
    params:
      data: predose_map
      variables: [AVAL]
```

::: {.notes}
A concrete payoff: filter with a workr-native SQL step, then summarize with
cards into an ARD. Two steps, one regulatory-grade result.
:::

## Persistence stays with you

- Workflows orchestrate transformation; saving is deliberately decoupled
- Writing to csv / parquet / json / a data lake is another step
- The same workflow can feed a Shiny app, a static site, or a PDF over email

::: {.notes}
Don't overclaim on storage — it's intentionally left to the organization. The
framework ends at "here is the derived object."
:::

# A side effect: it works well with AI {.center}

::: {style="opacity:0.8; font-size:0.85em;"}
a workflow is data, not code
:::

::: {.notes}
~18:00. We built workr for auditability. Because the logic is inspectable data,
it also turned out to be a good fit for agentic AI — for the same reason.
:::

## Agents can read and write workflows

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Read**

- Explain a workflow step by step
- Diff two runs and locate the change
- Debug a failure in plain language
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Write**

- Draft a new workflow from a request
- Add or reorder steps safely
- {gsm} + {workr} skills coming soon
:::
:::

The properties that make a workflow auditable also make it legible to a model.

::: {.notes}
Modular, inspectable steps are what agents handle well. This is a benefit we
noticed after the fact, not the original design goal.
:::

## New in {workr} 1.1.0

- **Project orchestration** — phase configs, continue-on-error, clearer
  diagnostics
- **Load/save hooks** — including GitHub Actions artifact providers to pass
  data between runs
- **Smarter discovery** — active/inactive filtering, priority ordering,
  exact-name matching

::: {style="font-size:0.72em; opacity:0.85; margin-top:0.4em;"}
These turn a set of workflows into a scheduled, restartable, multi-phase run.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ties back to the 27k-metrics story: orchestration and hooks are what make that
scale claim work in a regulated pipeline.
:::
